def lex_smallest_binary_matrix(row_sums, col_sums):
    """
    Reconstruct the lexicographically smallest binary matrix with the given
    row and column sums.

    You are given two lists of non-negative integers:
      - row_sums, of length m (1 <= m <= 30), with 0 <= row_sums[i] <= n
      - col_sums, of length n (1 <= n <= 30), with 0 <= col_sums[j] <= m

    A valid matrix is an m x n matrix of 0s and 1s in which row i contains
    exactly row_sums[i] ones and column j contains exactly col_sums[j] ones.

    Among all valid matrices, return the one that is lexicographically
    smallest when read row by row, left to right, as one long string of '0'
    and '1' characters (all candidates have equal length m*n, so this is
    plain string comparison). Return it as a list of m strings, each of
    length n, e.g. ['011', '100']. If no valid matrix exists, return [].
    The answer is unique, so no further tie-breaking is needed.

    Note: a single row alone can be filled in up to C(30, 15) > 1.5e8 ways,
    so enumerating row fillings or backtracking over cells is far too slow;
    you need an exact feasibility criterion to commit each cell greedily.

    >>> lex_smallest_binary_matrix([1, 1], [1, 1])
    ['01', '10']
    >>> lex_smallest_binary_matrix([2, 2], [2, 1, 1])
    ['101', '110']
    >>> lex_smallest_binary_matrix([3, 1], [2, 2, 0])
    []
